summary: Specifies the syntax of text messages sent between computer users as email, including the headers such as From and Date and the message body. It was on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 5322.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2822 defines how a text email is arranged so that mail systems can read its headers and body consistently. It specifies the header fields, their syntax and the line that separates the headers from the message text.

subtitle: The syntax for email headers and text bodies exchanged between computer users.

tldr.problem: Mail systems need a shared format for the headers and body of a text email message.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2822 defines ASCII message lines, header fields, a blank separator line, body text and formal grammar for field contents.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2822 obsoleted RFC 822 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 5322. It was also updated by RFCs 5335 and 5336.

today: RFC 2822 has been obsoleted by RFC 5322 and was updated by RFC 5335 and RFC 5336. It obsoleted RFC 822.

sections.title: Message Contents, Not Delivery
sections.content:
The RFC specifies syntax for text messages sent between computer users as email. It covers message contents, not the envelope information used to transmit and deliver a message.

The format does not define how a site stores messages, what mail features it must provide, or how a user interface behaves. Images, audio and other structured data require extensions outside this memo's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: This specification covers the contents of a text email, not how the mail system delivers it. Other specifications extend the format for images, audio and other data.

sections.title: Lines, Headers and the Body
sections.content:
A message uses US-ASCII characters in the range from 1 through 127. Lines end with a carriage return and line feed together, called CRLF. Header fields come first; an empty line separates them from the optional body.

Each line must be no longer than 998 characters and should be no longer than 78, excluding CRLF. A long header field can be folded across lines at permitted whitespace, then unfolded before the field is interpreted.
sections.plainLanguage: An email has header lines, an empty separator line and then its body. Long lines have defined limits, and a folded header is read as one field after its line break is removed.

sections.title: Required and Common Header Fields
sections.content:
The only required header fields are Date and From. If From lists more than one mailbox, Sender must also identify one mailbox. To lists primary recipients, Cc lists copied recipients and Bcc lists recipients whose addresses should not be revealed to others.

Message-ID should identify a particular message. In-Reply-To and References can connect a reply to earlier messages. Subject, Comments and Keywords provide human-readable information, while Received and Return-Path are trace fields added during delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: Date and From are the required headers. Other fields can identify recipients, give a subject, or help mail programs connect replies to earlier messages.

sections.title: Mailboxes and Addresses
sections.content:
An address can be a mailbox or a group of mailboxes. A mailbox may include a display name followed by an address in angle brackets, or it may appear as an address by itself.

A group has a display name followed by a colon, a list of mailboxes and a semicolon. Its list may be empty. The RFC defines the syntax of these addresses; the separate mail-transport specification defines how a message is routed to them.
sections.plainLanguage: A header can name one mailbox or a group of mailboxes. The syntax shows mail programs how to separate a display name, address and group members.

sections.title: Reading Obsolete Message Syntax
sections.content:
Section 4 describes syntax used by earlier versions or found in messages already in circulation. Message creators must not generate these obsolete forms, but conforming parsers must accept and interpret them.

The RFC also says that implementations should handle malformed messages robustly. A message that exceeds the specified line length is not a reason to silently discard the extra characters or lose the message.
sections.plainLanguage: New messages should use the current syntax. Mail programs must still understand older forms when they read a message.

sections.title: Display Risks and Blind Copies
sections.content:
Terminal escape sequences and other control characters can affect some terminals when a message is displayed. Viewers may remove dangerous sequences, but should not remove all escape sequences because some have valid uses.

Bcc handling can reveal confidential information, including that a person received a blind copy. Implementations must take care when processing replies so that a reply does not expose blind recipients.
sections.plainLanguage: Some control characters in a message can affect the device that displays it. Mail software must also handle Bcc carefully so that replying does not reveal a hidden recipient.
